pr.title: fix(core): serialize concurrent writes to the same order
pr.body:
Addresses the order concurrency issue #4152, and the races reported independently in #2187 and #3398.

Design note with the full reasoning is on #4152. Short version below, since it overturns the approach that issue proposes.

## Problem

Order mutations read an Order, change it in memory and write it back, with nothing coordinating concurrent requests. Two symptoms:

- **Lost updates and missing lines.** Concurrent mutations overwrite each other's columns.
- **Duplicate active orders.** Determining the active order is a check-then-act. Two concurrent first requests on one session each find nothing and each create an order.

Separately, stock allocation computed its new value in JavaScript from a value read a statement earlier, so two concurrent allocations of the same variant both read the same `stockAllocated` and one silently overwrote the other.

## Why not a version column

The issue proposes `@VersionColumn` on `Order` plus retry plus a partial unique index. That does not hold up here:

- **It would not fire on the main write path.** TypeORM checks a version only when saving a loaded entity carrying that version. `applyPriceAdjustments`, the most common Order-row writer, saves a field-omitted object; the address setters bypass the entity with a targeted `UPDATE`. The busiest paths would skip the check while looking protected in review.
- **Retry is not free.** Re-running a mutation body replays history entries, events and stock movements.
- **Partial indexes are not portable.** MySQL and MariaDB have no filtered indexes and both are in the required CI matrix.
- **It fixes neither the duplicate-order race nor the stock race**, both of which are check-then-act across different rows.

A row lock needs no schema change, no migration and no new error type, so this targets `master` as a bug fix.

## Fix

`TransactionalConnection.lockRow` takes a write lock on one row as a standalone `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` by primary key.

It deliberately does not lock a query that loads relations. Postgres rejects locking a left join, and switching the join to inner to satisfy it would change which rows the query returns. That was one of the review blockers on the earlier attempt in #4071.

It is a no-op in two cases:

- **Outside a transaction.** A lock taken in autocommit is released by the next statement and protects nothing. This is also what keeps read-only requests lock-free, since they are not wrapped by `@Transaction`.
- **On SQLite and sql.js.** No `FOR UPDATE` support, and no need for it: they serialize every write onto a single connection, so the race cannot occur. Three of the four CI database jobs still exercise the lock. Following the dialect-gating precedent in `default-scheduler-strategy.ts`.

The lock is taken in the two places every mutating path already goes through:

- `OrderService.getOrderOrThrow`, before the read it protects. Covers the admin and draft paths. Locks are idempotent within a transaction, so the repeated re-fetches in `addPaymentToOrder` cost nothing extra.
- `ActiveOrderService`, for the check-then-create. There is no order row to lock at that moment, so the lock goes on the Session, and on the User when the request is authenticated, since the fallback lookup for a logged-in customer is by user rather than by session. Every mutating shop resolver already carries `@Transaction()` and calls `getActiveOrder` inside it, so one site covers all of them.

`ctx.session` then has to be re-read from the database. It is a snapshot taken from the session cache when the request arrived, which is before the lock was granted, so an order created by the request we were waiting on is not visible in it. Without the re-read we would still go on to create a second order. This is the case @Lennix reported as still broken under the locking in #4071.

Locks are always taken in the order Session, User, Order, stated in the helper docblock, so two requests cannot deadlock by taking the same pair in opposite orders.

Stock levels now compute their change in SQL (`increment`), which is portable across all four databases and needs no lock. The insert branch of `updateStockOnHandForLocation` also handles losing the race to a concurrent insert, relying on the existing unique index on `stock_level`.

## Not covered

Nothing checks saleable stock at allocation time, so two orders can both buy the last unit. Allocation happens on the transition *out* of `ArrangingPayment`, and the only saleable-stock check is on the transition *into* it. This PR makes both allocations get recorded rather than one overwriting the other, which is the data-integrity half; the overselling itself is a separate gap and I'll open an issue for it.

I initially added a lock on the stock levels in the `ArrangingPayment` guard, then removed it: it guarded a check with no corresponding commit, so it cost contention and bought nothing.

## Tests

New `packages/core/e2e/order-concurrency.e2e-spec.ts`. Genuinely concurrent requests via `Promise.all`, following the precedent in `order-promotion.e2e-spec.ts`, discriminating on `__typename` rather than field shape. Skipped on sql.js with the reason stated.

Four of the five fail on `master`, deterministically: 4 runs, same 4 failures every time.

```
✓ does not lose an address written concurrently with a shipping method   (passes on master; pins the existing omit-list mitigation)
× adds every item when items are added concurrently                      expected [ 'T_3' ] to deeply equal [ 'T_1', 'T_2', 'T_3' ]
× adds every item when items are added concurrently to an existing order expected 349800 to be 719600
× creates exactly one order when a fresh session adds items concurrently expected 7 to be 5
× records every allocation when the last unit is paid for concurrently   expected 1 to be 2
```

### Each change is covered

An earlier version of this suite passed in full with the `getOrderOrThrow` lock reverted, meaning the lock at the centre of this PR was pinned by nothing. Every test started from an empty session, so the active order had to be created, the Session lock serialized the requests, and the Order lock was never what made them pass.

The fifth test closes that. It seeds an order first, so the Session lock is skipped and the Order lock is all that remains. Order lines are separate rows and survive on their own, so it asserts the order's `subTotal`, which each request recalculates from its own snapshot and writes to the same column.

Reverting each change in turn, on Postgres:

| Change reverted | Tests that fail |
| -- | -- |
| Lock in `getOrderOrThrow` | items added to an existing order |
| Lock in `ActiveOrderService` | items added concurrently; exactly one order |
| Session re-read after the lock | items added concurrently; exactly one order |
| SQL `increment` for stock levels | every allocation recorded |
| Nothing (full change) | none, 6 consecutive runs |

No part of this change can be removed without a test noticing.

## Verification

Postgres 16 unless noted:

| Suite | Result |
| -- | -- |
| `order-concurrency` | 5 passed, 6 consecutive runs; 4 fail on `master`, 4 consecutive runs |
| `order`, `shop-order`, `stock-control`, `order-promotion`, `parallel-transactions`, `database-transactions`, `draft-order` | 340 passed together with the new suite |
| Same suites on sql.js | pass, concurrency suite correctly skipped |
| Core unit tests | 1230 passed |

`tsc --noEmit` error count unchanged from `master`. Still to run on MySQL and MariaDB, which I don't have locally; CI covers both.

## Cost

Cart writes now serialize per order. Contention is bounded to one shopper's own cart, which has to serialize anyway. One lock at one place with a fixed acquisition order, rather than the seventeen scattered ones in #4071, so the deadlock surface stays small.

+    /**
+     * @description
+     * Takes a write lock on a single row, so that concurrent requests which want to modify the
+     * same row are serialized rather than overwriting each other. The lock is held until the
+     * surrounding transaction commits or rolls back.
+     *
+     * The lock is a standalone `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` by primary key. It deliberately does not
+     * load relations: locking a query which left-joins is rejected by Postgres, and making the
+     * join inner to satisfy it would silently change which rows the query returns.
+     *
+     * Two conditions have to hold, and the call is a no-op otherwise:
+     *
+     * * The database must support row locking. SQLite and sql.js do not, but they are also
+     *   single-connection, so the race a lock would prevent cannot occur on them.
+     * * The context must already be inside a transaction. A lock taken in autocommit is released
+     *   by the next statement and protects nothing, and this is what keeps read-only requests,
+     *   which are not wrapped by the {@link Transaction} decorator, from taking locks at all.
+     *
+     * When several rows are locked in one request, always lock them in the same order across the
+     * whole codebase, or two requests can deadlock by taking the same pair in opposite orders.
+     * The order used for order mutations is Session, then User, then Order.
+     *
+     * @since 3.7.3
+     */
+    async lockRow<T extends VendureEntity>(
+        ctx: RequestContext,
+        entityType: ObjectType<T>,
+        id: ID,
+    ): Promise<void> {
+        if (!ROW_LOCKING_DB_TYPES.includes(this.rawConnection.options.type)) {
+            return;
+        }
+        if (!this.getTransactionManager(ctx)) {
+            return;
+        }
+        await this.getRepository(ctx, entityType)
+            .createQueryBuilder('entity')
+            .select('entity.id')
+            .setLock('pessimistic_write')
+            .where('entity.id = :id', { id })
+            .getOne();
+    }
